doc.title: Chico Hamilton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The Dealer, Larry Coryell, and Bob Thiele's title
summary: Larry Coryell first listened to Gabor Szabo at the window of a Seattle club, then played in Hamilton's band; The Dealer album title came from Bob Thiele.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: So, yeah, you talked about this group. You had Jimmy Cheatham, Tom MacIntosh on trombone, and then two saxophones, Steve Potts and Arnie Lawrence. But you know there was a very similar recording made before that, The Dealer.
Oh, yeah, where I introduced Larry Coryell, yeah.
Right, let’s talk about that recording. That’s pretty funky.

Larry Coryell used to come here when we played Seattle, played the Playboy Club in Seattle. Larry was too young, he couldn’t come into the club but he used to come to the window and put his ear up against the window to listen to Gabor. Same thing with George Benson. Same thing in Pittsburgh. George flipped over Gabor. Well Gabor, man, was unbelievable, original, original, you dig? But anyway I got back to LA and all of a sudden Larry came into town and he called me and I put him on the band, you know, playing with Gabor, you know, that type of thing. So he wanted experience and that’s how that all happened. He ended up with -- we got to New York when I recorded -- Gabor left and Larry and Arnie came on the band and that’s how we did The Dealer.
So can you talk about that project? What was the inspiration for that project? Was that something that was your idea, your concept?

I didn’t have an idea about the title. George -- what’s his name, who’s the producer on that? Bob Thiele's idea, because I was smoking in those days, cigarettes, and that’s the reason they’ve got the cover with me smoking on it. There you go, look like a dealer.
Goddamn, ‘66, okay. I’ll tell you, that music stills holds up today don’t it?
